hook.text: Training a deep network is still maximum likelihood: find the weights that make the labels most probable. The difference is scale: many layers, millions of weights, and a gradient that must make it back through all of them.

plan.text: Fifteen questions: thirteen worked through, several on small digit networks, and two quick ones.

q1.text: Question one. What is a perceptron?

q1-a.text: A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, through an activation. Alone, it's a linear classifier: one straight line.

q1-xor.text: So it famously can't learn XOR, which is one when exactly one input is one: no line separates the ones from the zeros, and the best gets three of the four.
q1-xor.spoken: So it famously can't learn ex-or, which is one when exactly one input is one: no line separates the ones from the zeros, and the best gets three of the four.

q2.text: Question two. Why do we need non-linear activation functions? Add two hidden units with ReLU, which zeroes negatives, and XOR comes out exactly: zero, one, one, zero.
q2.spoken: Question two. Why do we need non-linear activation functions? Add two hidden units with ReLU, which zeroes negatives, and ex-or comes out exactly: zero, one, one, zero.

q2-collapse.text: Take the ReLU out, and the same weights collapse to one linear function, minus each input, plus two: one line again. Without a non-linearity, stacked layers are one layer; with one, a wide network can approximate almost any function.

q3.text: Question three. Compare sigmoid, tanh, and ReLU.

q3-sat.text: Sigmoid maps to zero to one, tanh to minus one to one, centered on zero. Both flatten at the ends, passing almost no gradient: the page's code finds sigmoid's slope peaks at a quarter, and tanh's, peaking at one, is point oh seven by an input of two.

q3-relu.text: ReLU's slope is one for any positive input, it costs one comparison, and it's the default for hidden layers. The catch: a unit whose input is always negative outputs zero, gets zero gradient, and never recovers.

q3-fix.text: Leaky ReLU keeps a small slope below zero; ELU and GELU bend smoothly, and GELU is the usual choice in transformers. Softmax belongs at a multi-class output.
q3-fix.spoken: Leaky ReLU keeps a small slope below zero; ee-loo and GELU bend smoothly, and GELU is the usual choice in transformers. Softmax belongs at a multi-class output.

q4.text: Question four. Explain backpropagation and the chain rule.

q4-a.text: The forward pass computes each layer and keeps its activations. The backward pass runs from the loss down, multiplying local derivatives, so every weight gets its gradient in one sweep.

q4-cost.text: This digit network has twenty-six thousand parameters. Nudging each to measure its effect takes twenty-six thousand forward passes per step. Backprop takes one, plus a backward pass worth one point seven, counting multiply-adds.

q4-check.text: Nudging is still how you test a backward pass: on twenty weights here, the two agree to better than one part in a million.

q4-memory.text: The price is memory: kept activations grow with batch size and depth, so training takes far more memory than serving.

q5.text: Question five. What causes vanishing and exploding gradients, and how do you fix them? That backward sweep is a long product: factors mostly below one, and the gradient vanishes; mostly above, it explodes.

q5-sim.text: Simulate twenty layers of a hundred and twenty-eight units. With sigmoid, under a trillionth of the gradient reaches the first layer, so early layers barely learn. With ReLU and He initialization, it arrives about the size it left.

q5-explode.text: Start the same ReLU network with weights twice as spread out, and it arrives over a million times larger. The updates blow up, and the loss becomes not a number.

q5-fix.text: The fixes: ReLU-family activations, careful initialization, residual connections, which give the gradient a path with a derivative of one, and normalization. For explosions, clip: past a threshold, scale the gradient down, keeping its direction.

q5-watch.text: Log the gradient norm every training step: a slide toward zero, or a spike before the loss breaks, shows there first.

q6.text: Question six. Why does weight initialization matter? Xavier versus He.

q6-a.text: That explosion was the starting scale alone. Xavier sets the variance to two over inputs plus outputs, for tanh and sigmoid; He, two over inputs, since ReLU zeroes half of what it sees.

q6-sym.text: And never start the weights equal. Sixteen hidden units started at point oh one end a thousand steps as exact copies, one unit in effect, scoring thirty-eight percent on held-out digits. From Xavier's random start, ninety-eight.

q6-why.text: Equal units get equal gradients, so nothing ever breaks the tie.

norm-in.text: Normalization keeps that scale steady in training.

q7.text: Question seven. What is batch normalization, and how does layer norm differ?

q7-a.text: Batch norm shifts and scales each feature to mean zero and variance one across the mini-batch, then applies a learned scale and shift.

q7-batch.text: So the answer depends on the neighbors. This pixel, at half brightness, normalizes to minus two point four beside seven brighter digits, and to plus two point six beside seven darker ones.

q7-one.text: In a batch of one, a feature is its own mean, so it normalizes to zero whatever the input; hence running averages at inference. Left in training mode and served one request at a time, that layer ignores its input.

q7-ln.text: Layer norm normalizes across one example's features instead: this pixel gets the same value in any batch, or alone. Free of batch size, it's what transformers use.

q8.text: Question eight. What is the difference between SGD, Momentum, RMSProp, and Adam?

q8-a.text: Stochastic gradient descent steps against each mini-batch's gradient. Momentum keeps a decaying average of past gradients, which damps the zigzag.

q8-rms.text: RMSProp divides each parameter's step by the root of a running average of its squared gradients; Adam does both. Give two parameters gradients a hundred times apart: SGD's steps are a hundred and four times apart, Adam's, one point oh three.

q8-mem.text: The follow-up is memory. In thirty-two-bit floats, a weight and its gradient take eight bytes; momentum adds four, Adam eight. A billion weights need eight gigabytes with SGD and sixteen with Adam, before any activations.

q8-choice.text: Adam is the usual default; well-tuned SGD with momentum often generalizes slightly better on vision, in a quarter less memory.

reg-in.text: A network that trains well can still memorize.

q9.text: Question nine. Explain dropout, L2, and early stopping as regularizers.

q9-a.text: Dropout zeroes a random share of units each training step, commonly a fifth to a half, so none can rely on particular others. Survivors are usually scaled up in training, so at inference it's simply off.

q9-bug.text: Leave it on in a digit classifier trained with it. Ten calls on one image of an eight: eight say eight, at forty-eight to ninety-three percent, and two say one. Across the test set, one image in ten changes its answer within ten calls.

q9-dash.text: Yet accuracy only slips from ninety-eight to ninety-seven percent, so no dashboard flags it. Check that serving runs in evaluation mode, and that one input gets one output.

q9-l2.text: L2 penalizes squared weights, pulling them toward zero. With plain SGD that's the same as weight decay; with Adam it isn't, so decay the weights directly. Early stopping keeps the weights from the best validation epoch, and all three limit what a network can memorize.

cnn-in.text: Then, architectures shaped to their data.

q10.text: Question ten. How does a convolutional neural network, or CNN, work?

q10-a.text: It slides small learned filters over the image, each computing a local weighted sum. This three-by-three filter lights up on a handwritten zero's vertical edges.

q10-props.text: Each output sees a small patch through one shared filter, so a pattern is found anywhere: shift the digit two pixels right, and the map shifts with it. Pooling then shrinks it, tolerating small shifts.

q11.text: Question eleven. Why are CNNs well suited to images compared to a fully-connected net?

q11-a.text: Count weights. For a color image two hundred and twenty-four pixels square, a dense layer to a thousand units needs a hundred and fifty million; the page's first convolution, four hundred and forty-eight.

q11-cost.text: The page's whole network has five thousand four hundred and eighteen. But its first layer reuses each weight at fifty thousand positions: twenty-two million multiply-adds, cheap to store, not to compute.

q11-bias.text: That built-in assumption, that nearby pixels belong together, is why a CNN needs far less data.

r-transfer.text: Transfer learning: start from a pretrained network. With little data, freeze it and train a new head; with more, fine-tune some or all layers. It cuts data and compute, and one frozen backbone can serve many heads.

r-softmax.text: Why pair softmax with cross-entropy? Their combined gradient is prediction minus target, large exactly when the model is confidently wrong. Libraries fuse them on raw logits, so don't apply softmax first: applied twice over ten classes, the right class tops out at twenty-three percent, and the loss can't drop below one point four six.

q14.text: Question fourteen. What is an RNN, and why does it struggle with long sequences?

q14-a.text: A recurrent neural network reads a sequence one step at a time, updating one hidden state with the same weights each step.

q14-why.text: So the gradient from step fifty back to step one passes through fifty similar factors. If each halves it, one part in a thousand trillion is left: long-range patterns are forgotten, or, with factors above one, they explode.

q14-slow.text: And step fifty can't start until step forty-nine is done, so a GPU can't work on a sequence's steps in parallel.

q15.text: Question fifteen. How do LSTMs and GRUs address that?

q15-a.text: The LSTM, or long short-term memory, adds a cell state changed mostly by addition, under input, forget and output gates. Along it, the gradient meets only the forget gate: at point nine five, fifty steps keep about eight percent.

q15-gru.text: The GRU, gated recurrent unit, uses two gates and no separate cell: three blocks of weights to the LSTM's four, for similar results.

q15-limit.text: But both still read one step at a time.

next.text: Attention did it better: every position reaches every other in one step, all at once, and language models are built on it. Next: NLP and large language models.
